5. Defendant Nos. 3-7 supports defendant No. 2 and claim that after their purchase of 3/8 share they got their names mutated in the revenue records and have been paying rent to the government and obtained dakhilas. Due to gradual recession of river further land were added to their purchased land on the north and south of mouza Tetultala and this accreted land are shown in block Nos. 6 and 7 of the Collector's map and defendant Nos. 2-7 and their predecessors had been peacefully possessing those lands as accretion to the tenancies along with Zohura Khatun, the transferee, for more than 12 years till the date of attachment of the same by the government; that the bargadars of these defendants grew paddy in 1363 BS but some unknown persons claiming settlement from government cut and took away the paddy with the help of police. They instituted Title Suit Nos. 18, 19 and 78 of 1958 in the Court of Subordinate Judge, Khulna due to, the attachment of the land by the government praying for declaration of their tenancy right in these lands and for damages and the said suits have been stayed till disposal of the present suit. 

 6. Defendant No. 8 Nalini Bala Devi in her written statement alleges that on the formation of the chars in the northern and southern side of mouza Tetultala immediately after CS operation the owners of the adjacent asli land had been in possession of these char lands as accretion to their holding and there was no apprehension of breach of peace. She further states that one Asor Sarder and another Hosaain Sarder had raiyati tenancy recorded in khatian No. 69 under Kailash Chandra Chatterjee and others and one Nistarini Devi took settlement of the land of this khatian No. 69 from Asor Sarker and Hosaain Sarder in 1341 BS; subsequently Nistarini Devi executed a deed of gift in favour of defendant No. 8 on 2.11.43. When Asor and his co-sharer's interest was put to rent sale defendant No. 8 auction-purchased it to save her interest in Rent Execution case No. 1264 of 1943. This auction- purchase was made in the benami of Shushila Bala Devi, who was her daughter-in-law. She further states that river Kazibacha lies to the north of defendant No. 8's land of Dag No. 170 of Khatian No. 69 and with the gradual recession of the river there had been accretion to her land to the extent of about 60 bighas which she had been possessing through her bargadars for more than 12 years and the Collector has illegally attached that land; that she had filed Title Suit No. 39 of 1957 in the Court of Subordinate Judge, Khulna for declaration of her title and for damage which is still pending. 

 8. Further case of defendant No. 9 is that he has tenancy right in CS Plot No.3 along with other land at a rental of Rs. 35.00 which he took lease of by executing kabuliyat dated 21.5.37 in favour of Nalini Bala Chatterjee, who annulled all the subordinate interest under section 167 of the Bengal Tenancy Act and defendant No. 9 had been possessing since then. Due to recession of the river Kazibacha chars accreted to CS Plot Nos. 3.4,8,9, 11 and Diara Plot Nos. 633, 160, 244; 169, 162, 163, 164 and 169 and CS Plot Nos. 634, 170 and 17l. These accreted land were surveyed in 1940 and depicted in the TS Nos. 51, 52, 53 and 54 which has been shown in Diara map and the Collector's map as well. During the said survey there were accretions to CS Plot Nos. 3, 4, 7, 8, 9 and 101 of estate No. 120 but the land accreted to them were not surveyed at the time of Diara survey in 1940. For these accreted land defendant No. 2 brought suits for additional rent for additional areas against Nalini Bala and others and obtained decrees. Thereafter there were further accretion to CS Plot Nos. 3.4,7,8, 9 and 101 and the owners of the riparian land were possessing the said land as parts of their tenancies. Defendant No. 9 had been possessing the land accreted to CS Plot No. 3 till the date of attachment and the Government at best can claim enhanced rent for the addition of area of the tenancy. 

 9. The case of defendant No. 21 Zohura Khatun is that during CS operation a Diara proceeding was started and it was found that these were Diara land which were assigned new Touzi No. 1144. The proprietors of Touzi No. 120 along with their tenants obtained settlement of the Diara land which were delineated in the map prepared in 1940 and new khatians were opened in the names of those who held contiguous asli land. Her further case is that she purchased PS Plot Nos. 113 and 114 and portion of plot No. 115 of Khatian No. 24 by kabala dated 16.11.33 AD from Satish Chandra Bhadra who was a tenant under defendant No. 2 and who held a tenure under Touzi No. 1144. Some soft char formed in the contiguous land and there was accretion to plot Nos. 113 and 114 but these were not included in her kabala. She, however, began to cultivate those accreted land since they became fit for cultivation and then settled some of those lands to bargadars and the land yielded 30 maunds of paddy per year. She further states that the khal or the canal as shown between Block Nos. 6 and 7 of Collector's map was fordable at the time of formation of the char and it does not exist now. That for mala fide intention the khal has been shown in the map. She further alleges that there is an island char to the immediate cast of plot No. 7 and this char is known as Touzi No. 1144. That the owner of the touzi cannot claim block No. 7. That the lands accreted to the land of Touzi 1444 shown in block No.6 and portion of block No.7 are part and parcel of their respective tenancies. The accreted land of defendant No. 21 is lower than those of defendant Nos. 2-7. In short, defendant No. 21 claims tenancy right in the land which accreted to plot Nos. 113 and 114 and so the government, according to her, can claim additional rent. 

 23. Mr. Moazzem Hossain, the learned Deputy Attorney-General at the outset has taken the legal objection that the suit as well as the present appeal, which is the continuation of the suit, is not at all maintainable and should abate in view of the provisions of sections 86 and 87 of the State Acquisition & Tenancy Act, 1950 as amended by PO Nos. 72, 135 and 137 of 1972. His next contention is that the islands which are the subject matter of the dispute arose out of the bed of the navigable river Kazibacha and as such those have vested in the government in accordance with the provision of law and therefore, no one else can set up any claim over the same. 

 24. At the very outset we would like to dispose of the legal objection taken by the learned Deputy Attorney-General. Sections 86 and 87 of the State Acquisition & Tenancy Act as amended by PO Nos. 72, 135 and 137 of 1972 introduced radical changes in the century old law with respect to land gained by the recess of river or of the sea, as well as land reformed in situ, by providing that such accreted land or reformed land not be considered as the land of riparian or the original owner, as the case may be, but shall vest in the government free from all encumbrances, unless such accretion or reformation was finally recognised or declared by a competent authority or Court under any law for the time being in force. This provision of law was also given retrospective effect by insertion of the words "whether the loss of such land or portion by diluvion took or takes place before or after the commencement of State Acquisition &Tenancy (Fourth Amendment) Order, 1972. This fourth amendment is incorporated in PO 135 of 1972. In sub-section (3) similar provisions have been made with respect to land reformed in situ. Sub-section (5) of this amended section 86 further provides that all suits, applications, appeals or other proceeding with respect to any claim to the re-possession of any land lost by diluvion which has re-appeared or is alleged to have re-appeared pending before any Court or authority on the date of commencement of the said PO 135 of 1972 shall not proceed and shall abate. Mr. Moazzem Hossain relying on the provisions of this amended law as contained in sub-sections (2), (3) and (5) of section 86 contends that admittedly the disputed land are accretions as claimed by some of the defendants or reformation in situ as claimed by others and since the litigation with respect to title and possession over the said land was pending on the date of coming into force of PO 135 of 1972 the present appeal, which is a continuation of the original suit, cannot proceed and should abate. This contention of the learned Deputy Attorney-General may appear correct on the face of the provisions contained in statute itself. However, every law must be looked into not only by the language appearing in the statute book but also by its interpretation as enunciated by the superior courts of the country. Our Constitution enjoins that the decisions of the highest court i.e. the Supreme Court of Bangladesh should be followed and acted upon by all authorities and subordinate Courts. A decision given by the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court is binding upon all Courts including the High Court Division. In the case of Abdul Mannan Vs. Kulada Ranjan Mowali reported in 31 DLR (AD) 195, their Lordships of the Appellate Division after discussing the history of the development of the law relating to accretion and reformation-in-situ as well as the provisions of sections 86 and 87 of the State Acquisition & Tenancy Act, 1950 as amended in 1972 have held: 

 25. Thus after the above quoted pronouncement of the Appellate Division (31 DLR page 195) there remains no doubt about the fact that the provision of sections (2), (3) and (5) of section 87 as they stand now, can have effect only with respect to land which have accreted or re-appeared after Part V of the State Acquisition & Tenancy Act, 1950 came into force in the locality in question. In the District of Khulna Part V of the Act came into force on August 29, 1963 whereas the disputed land appeared above the water of the river as hard soil due to recession of the river Kazibacha in the later part of the forties or in the early part of the fifties and attached by the Collector in 1955. In these circumstances the amended provision of sections 86 and 87 can in no way be applicable in the instant case. Therefore, the contention of the learned Deputy Attorney-General is not tenable in the eye of law. 

 26. Mr. Khondker Mahbubuddin Ahmed has raised objection as regards the correctness of the sketch-map prepared by the Collector and appended to the letter of reference. We find that at the time of trial the District Kanungo of Khulna ABM Moslemuddin was examined as PW 1 on behalf of the government represented by the Collector of Khulna, He deposed to the effect that after attachment of the disputed land the Collector ordered for survey of the same and accordingly Amin Abdul Masud Chowdhury surveyed and then Kanungo Monjur Ali prepared the map. On perusal of the said map it appears that the revenue survey lines as well as the channels have been depicted therein. From Ext. I, it also appears that on the application of one Haran Chand Mallik the Collector of Khulna started Misc. Case. No. 54 of 1957 and in that case the map was prepared by the Government Surveyor. Moreover, on scrutiny of the sketch map it becomes crystal clear that it contains the entire land in dispute and it has been sufficiently identified. Moreover, the original two island chars, the accreted land, khals, revenue survey lines and all other salient features of the disputed property have been clearly depicted in the map. So we find that the learned Subordinate Judge rightly came to the finding that there was no defect in the sketch map relating to the disputed land prepared under the order of the Collector and appended to the letter of reference. The law relating to chars or alluvial land is laid down in the Bengal Alluvion and Diluvion Regulations, 1825 (Regulation No. XI of 1825). The first clause of section 4 of Regulation XI of 1825 provides: 

 Thus the law as it was in force at the relevant time provided that all alluvial land would be increment to the land of the Zaminder or tenant who held the main land under any superior landlord including the government. No doubt in the third clause it has been provided that if a char is thrown opened in a large navigable river the bed of which is not the property of any individual and if the channels of the river between the char and the main land are not fordable it shall be at the disposal of the government, but if the channel is fordable in any season of the year it shall be acquisition to the land of the persons whose estate may be most contiguous to it. Relying on this provision of law, the leaned Deputy Attorney-General Mr. Moazzem Hossain contends that it is admitted by almost all the contending parties in the suit that two island chars arose out of the bed of the river Kazibacha which was navigable at the relevant time and the two chars have been depicted as 'A' in the sketch map, in that view of the matter, according to him, these two chars belong to the government as per provision of clause (3) of section 4 of regulation XI of 1825 and any accretion to these two chars are accretion to government khas land and no one else can set forth claim over them. There is no doubt about the fact that PWs 1 and 2 as well as OWs 1-6 who were witnesses for defendant Nos. 2-7 in unequivocal language stated that in or around 1940 two island chars, one described as the northern char comprising of 2.55 acres, and the other as the southern char comprising 16.60 acres arose out of the bed of the river Kazibacha running through mouza Tetultala. DW 8 Mansur Bawali who is defendant No. 22, DW 9 Hatem Ahmed who deposed on behalf of defendant Nos. 9 and 12-18, DW 10 Tarek Mondal who deposed on behalf of defendant No. 21 also supported the case of the government and DWs 1-6 about the raising of these two chars out of the bed of the river which belonged to nobody. Therefore, there remains no doubt about the fact that immediately after the formation of these two island chars marked 'A' in the sketch map, those were at the disposal of the government. But it is the case of the defendant No. 2 and others that he, Kali Kanta Chatterjee, Anil Kumar Ghosh and Bhupendra Nath Das took lease of both the Chars in their totality from the government by executing four kabuliyats. The kabuliyat executed by Kali Kanta Chaterjee has not been produced in Court as because in spite of being called for the government who is supposed to be in custody of the same, did not file it. But the other three kabuliyats executed in the year 1946 have been filed in Court and marked as A, A(1) and A(2). These three documents prove that defendant Abdul Haque Sarker, Anil Kumar Ghosh and Bhupendra Nath Das executed kabuliyat in favour of the government for 4.79 acres of land each of the two island chars. Mr. Moazzem Hossain tried to argue that mere execution of the kabuliyats cannot create tenancy in favour of these executants unless the same were accepted by the government and the executants were recognised as tenants. But the documents Ext. A, A(I) and A(2) show that these were accepted by Khas Mohal Officer, Khulna and the said Officer also attested the same as witness. Moreover, these sets of defendants filed series of dakhilas to prove that they paid rent to the government for their leased land. So there cannot be any doubt about the fact that the two chars after becoming cultivable, were leased out by the government to defendant No. 1 Abdul Haque Sarder, Kali Kanta Chatterjee, Haran Kumar Ghosh and Bhupendra Nath Das in 1946 and subsequently rent was also accepted from them. With the leasing out of the land these four persons became tenure holders under the government and therefore on and from date of their acquisition of lease hold right over the two island chars clause (1) of section 4 of Regulation XI of 1825 became operative and by virtue of that provision of law they became entitled to anyadditional land which was gained to the two original island chars by recession of the river as increment to their tenure. Under the circumstances the plea taken by the government that since the two original chars marked 'A' in the Collector's sketch map, belonged to the government any accretion to them would automatically vest in the government is unacceptable. These accretions by operation of law as was in force at the time of such accretion, went to the tenure holders and their under tenants as well as the transferees as increment to their holdings. Of course, if the other set of defendants namely defendant Nos. 24-25, 26, 27, 30, 31-37 and 38-39 could show that these newly risen lands were reformation in situ of their land which previously were diluviated, then their claim would get preference. The documents filed in the trial Court show that by Ext. B one of the lease holders Kali Kanta Chatterjee, leased out his share to defendant No. 3, Sk. Nuruddin, that defendant No. 4, Emdad Ali Khan purchased the share for Buhpendra by kabala Ext. F and one Mahbubur Rahman purchased this interest of Anil Kumar by Ext. F(2) who in turn sold it to defendant Nos. 5-7 by Ext. F(1). These persons possessed their respective land in the islands and paid rent to the government and obtained dakhilas marked Ext. B series. The sketch map also shows that the accreted lands which are subject matter of the dispute depicted as blocks 1 to 5, surround the original northern island char of 2.55 acres while block Nos. 6 and 7 are contiguous to original southern island char of 16.60 acres and those have been attached by the Collector, being subject matter of contention between the parties and cause of apprehension of breach of peace. It may also be mentioned here that the kabuliyats marked Ext. A to A(2) contained the stipulation that in case of increase in the area of four lease hold lands the lessees would be liable to pay increased rent. This stipulation in other words means that the lessees would be entitled to any accretion that may happen to the areas of the original leased out land. In the Collector's map two khals or channels have been shown, one running between the block Nos. 2 and 3 and the other one between the block Nos. 6 and 7. PW 1, the District Kanungo tried to make out a case that these khals were navigable but he could not give the exact depth of the khals and on the other hand, he admitted that he had no personal knowledge of the origin of the khals or if they were fordable or not. On the other hand, DW 1 categorically stated that the khals were fordable at the time of formation of the disputed chars and that subsequently those have further silted up. Defendant Nos. 2-11, 12-18 and 21 and 23 claimed the disputed land as accretion to their tenancies.
